episode.throughLine: An enslaved sailor’s route is changed and an expected reward fails; after selling his own goods he asks how to present the price for freedom, faces the owner backing away, and obtains a release with the captain’s intervention.

contentProfile.contentNote: Enslavement and coerced shipping, care for a dying man and his death, failed payment, threatened withdrawal of promised freedom, and racial violence after manumission. The fight and threat are stated without graphic detail. Savings do not guarantee freedom.

facts.statement: Equiano reports birth in 1745 in chapter I; the 1766 episode therefore implies about 20–21. The birth year is self-reported and must remain approximate; no birthplace claim is used.

sourceRefs.locator: I: I was born, in the year 1745; VII: beginning of the year 1766 and reproduced July manumission.

facts.statement: Early in 1766 he sold goods on a voyage and hoped selling them after returning to Montserrat would provide enough to purchase freedom.

sourceRefs.locator: VII: Every day now brought me nearer through I should have enough to purchase my freedom.

facts.statement: The owner ordered the vessel to other ports instead of returning home; Equiano was disappointed and could not invest all his money as profitably at the new stop.

sourceRefs.locator: VII: But, as soon as our vessel arrived through remainder I brought away with me neat.

facts.statement: On that voyage the vessel also carried enslaved people; his personal trading unfolded within this coercive shipping system.

sourceRefs.locator: VII: After we had discharged our cargo there we took in a live cargo.

facts.statement: A silversmith became gravely ill; the captain attended him and promised Equiano extra pay after receiving the man’s property. After the death they eagerly opened a nest of trunks. Papers in the smallest were mistaken for valuable notes and the captain clapped his hands. Examination found that the whole nest held only one dollar and a half; all the property could not pay for a coffin. Both men went away mortified. Equiano had nearly enough to purchase freedom even before the anticipated bonus.

sourceRefs.locator: Chapter VII, A silversmith through We went away greatly mortified; especially I thought this would be of great service, although I had nearly money enough; At last; The whole amount.

facts.statement: After returning and selling his goods, he had about 47 pounds and asked the captain how to present the agreed 40-pound sterling purchase price.

sourceRefs.locator: VII: We set sail once more for Montserrat through consult my true friend.

facts.statement: The captain told him to come one morning when he and the owner were having breakfast together.

sourceRefs.locator: VII: He told me to come on a certain morning.

facts.statement: He entered with money in his hand and fear in his heart, bowed, and asked the owner to keep his promise of freedom when he could pay.

sourceRefs.locator: VII: Accordingly, on that morning through as soon as I could purchase it.

facts.statement: The owner recoiled from the request; Equiano heart sank, and the owner questioned whether he had the money and how he earned it.

sourceRefs.locator: VII: This speech seemed to confound him through How did you get it.

facts.statement: Equiano explained honestly how he obtained the money; the captain confirmed honest earnings and industry.

sourceRefs.locator: VII: I told him, very honestly through particularly careful.

facts.statement: The owner said Equiano had gained money faster than he had and that he would not have made the promise had he expected savings so quickly.

sourceRefs.locator: VII: On which my master replied through got money so soon.

facts.statement: At breakfast the captain clapped the owner on the back and urged him to keep the freedom promise and accept payment. He argued that the owner had already profited from Equiano’s work, was now receiving his purchase money back, and could still save money because Equiano would remain with the vessels.

sourceRefs.locator: Chapter VII, Come, come, said my worthy Captain through Come, Robert, take the money.

facts.statement: The owner said he would keep the promise, accepted the money, and sent Equiano to obtain a written release.

sourceRefs.locator: VII: My master then said through get my manumission drawn up.

facts.statement: His fear turned to joy; he bowed, cried, thanked the men, and left the room to obtain the document.

sourceRefs.locator: VII: These words of my master through left the room.

facts.statement: He paid for the document at the register office and took it back to be signed; the owner signed it that day.

sourceRefs.locator: VII: When I got to the office through he signed the manumission that day.

facts.statement: The reproduced document was signed July 10, 1766 and registered July 11, 1766. It records 70 pounds in island currency; his narrative states 40 pounds sterling. These are distinct currency labels, not contradictory purchase amounts.

sourceRefs.locator: Chapter VII reproduced manumission: consideration sum, hand and seal dating clause, and registration statement.

facts.statement: He remained with the vessel as a paid able-bodied sailor, though he wanted to return to England.

sourceRefs.locator: VII: So that my worthy captain through entered on board as an able-bodied sailor.

facts.statement: During the next voyage in August 1766, an enslaved man insulted and struck him; he lost his temper and beat the man. The other man’s owner threatened to have him publicly flogged. He refused to come ashore and, after repeated advice, hid at a friend’s house. The vessel was searched after he left.

sourceRefs.locator: Chapter VII, During our stay at this place through I was secreted about five days.

facts.statement: Friends demanded return of the warrant before he resumed work; he paid the expenses and returned aboard.

sourceRefs.locator: VII: Some of my other friends then asked through went on board again to my work.

facts.statement: His published autobiography records his enslavement and freedom, and he advocated against slavery.

sourceRefs.locator: Title page: The Interesting Narrative written by himself; I opening publication purpose; XII petition to the Queen on behalf of enslaved Africans.

arc.canonicalText:
He was back in port when the owner came aboard the loaded vessel. He was about twenty-one. He had been selling goods during the voyage. He hoped selling his goods here could leave him enough to purchase his freedom. The man giving the orders owned him as well as the vessel.

The owner ordered them to unload at another port, then sail on again. He was disappointed. He could not choose where the vessel went. His goods were still on board.
arc.sourceNote: Chapter VII owner boarding and route order. One loaded vessel in port. Age is approximate from the self-reported birth year. No exact cargo, port name, period identifier, or unrecorded instruction is added.

arc.canonicalText:
In the house, he and the captain opened the smallest trunk. There were papers inside. They thought the papers were valuable notes. They had taken the trunks out of one another, expecting to find money. The man they had been caring for was dead. He had promised the captain a large amount of money. The captain had promised him extra pay for helping attend the man.

The captain had clapped his hands when they first saw the papers. They examined what they had found. The whole set of trunks held only a little money. All the man’s possessions could not even pay for his coffin. The payment he had expected was gone. Now he and the captain were bitterly disappointed. They went away from the trunks.
arc.sourceNote: Chapter VII, trunk examination after the silversmith’s death. One encounter in the house. Expected notes prove to be little money; reported mortification supplies the feeling. He already had nearly enough savings, so this failure is not portrayed as destroying every prospect.

arc.canonicalText:
He asked the captain how to offer the owner the money for his freedom. They had returned to the port, unloaded the vessel, and he had sold his goods. He now had more than the price the owner had named. His trading had taken place aboard a vessel that also carried people held in slavery.

The owner’s earlier offer was to free him once he could pay. The captain told him to come one morning when he and the owner were having breakfast together. He could make the request then.
arc.sourceNote: Chapter VII, We set sail once more: after selling goods he consults the captain about offering the money. One conversation; exact room and gestures are unspecified and not invented. Past earnings and the completed voyage’s coerced shipping context are brief background; no unrecorded moral realization is assigned.

arc.canonicalText:
That morning, he entered with the money in his hand. He was afraid. He bowed and asked the owner to keep the promise. The owner drew back from the request. He felt discouraged. The owner asked whether he had the whole amount, and where it had come from. He answered honestly about how he had earned it.

The captain confirmed that he had earned it through work and careful trading. The owner said he had gained money faster than he had himself. He said he would never have promised freedom if he had expected such quick payment. The money was in the room. The owner was still questioning the release.
arc.sourceNote: Chapter VII, Accordingly, on that morning through got money so soon. Breakfast request, questioning, his truthful answer, and the owner’s stated regret. This follows the consultation chronologically and contains no voyage flashback.

arc.canonicalText:
The captain clapped the owner on the back and pressed him to accept the money. He argued that the owner had already profited from the young man’s work. Now the price he had paid for him was being returned. He also said the young man could remain with the vessels and save him money. The captain asked him to keep the freedom promise.

The owner agreed to keep the promise. He took the money and told him to have a written release prepared. His fear turned to joy. He bowed, with tears flowing before he could express all he felt. The captain congratulated them both. After the first strong feelings of joy passed, he thanked the two men. Then he rose and left the room to have his release prepared.
arc.sourceNote: Chapter VII, Come, come through left the room. One breakfast encounter: back-clap, economic pressure, acceptance, tears, thanks and leaving for paperwork. Captain help does not erase owner control or the economics of enslavement.

arc.canonicalText:
An official prepared the release for a fee. He paid and took it back for the owner to sign. The document was signed that day and registered the next. He had legal freedom now. He wanted to go elsewhere, but agreed to remain with the vessel. From that day he worked as a sailor for wages.

On the next voyage, another man struck him, and he struck back. That man’s owner threatened to have him beaten in public. He refused to come ashore. After repeated advice, he hid at a friend’s house. Friends insisted that the warrant be withdrawn before he returned. He had to pay the expenses. Then he went back aboard to work.
arc.sourceNote: Chapter VII document, paid sailor entry, and August altercation, concealment, warrant and return. Legal signing and registration retain separate dates in the used fold fact. Both the assault against him and his retaliation are stated; no graphic detail is added.

arc.canonicalText:
His name was Olaudah Equiano.

He wrote an account of his life in slavery and freedom that became part of the argument against slavery.

Your life is not theirs. But a piece of this story may still sit beside you.

You do not have to know how it ends to keep going. You are allowed to feel uncertain about what comes next.
arc.sourceNote: Primary title page and abolition petition supply the plain legacy. Name, one known-for sentence, fixed distance pair, and two authored permissions. No invented texture or promise.

dramatizationLimits: No invented events, dates, dialogue, motives, or causal links.
Interior states and sensory particulars only where the memoir explicitly reports them.
This draft uses no quotation and no invented texture.
avoidRules: Do not say savings alone secured freedom; the owner controlled release and the captain intervened.
Do not describe the owner as a liberator free of participation in enslavement.
Do not relabel chapter VI incidents as 1765; its ending explicitly dates them 1764.
Do not collapse July 10 signature and July 11 registration.
Do not confuse 40 pounds sterling with 70 pounds island currency.
Do not present self-reported 1745 birth or an African birthplace as an independently resolved fact.
Do not promise that work or saving can produce freedom under enslavement.
Do not omit the continued racial threats after legal manumission.

sources.citation: Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative (1789), chapters I and VII, including the reproduced manumission.
sources.locator: I: self-reported 1745 birth. VII: beginning 1766 voyage, detour, silversmith promise, breakfast request, Register Office and July 10/11 manumission; August 1766 threat and resulting concealment.
